column2: Against the trench sides; formwork is needed only if near-vertical trench sides do not stand in the granular soil.
For the same footing width, a reinforced concrete strip footing can be shallower than an unreinforced one.
That is why it is advantageous when the footing depth is limited.
Partition walls do not need separate foundations, because they carry only themselves.
They do need foundations: a separate strip footing, a thickened floor slab or a reinforced concrete beam.
For a pad foundation, the B/L ratio is usually between 1 and 3.5.
Most often it is square in plan.
The holding-down bolts of a steel column serve to transfer any tensile forces.
They can also provide a moment-resisting connection in one or two directions.
A continuous beam foundation reduces differential settlements in both directions.
Only in one direction; in both directions it is the beam-grid foundation.
Because they are relatively thin, raft foundations are usually very flexible.
They can be stiffened with ribs.
A mushroom (flat-slab) type raft serves to prevent punching.
In framed buildings, with larger loads.
For a ground-bearing raft, the underside of the slab may stay above the frost depth.
It is placed on a well-compacted granular bedding layer at least 50–60 cm thick.
Shell foundations are still often used today because they save material.
They need a lot of labour and time and did not prove economical – they are no longer used.
Structurally, a box foundation can be regarded as a box girder.
The base slab, the basement walls and the floor form a monolithic whole.
Before designing the foundations, it has to be checked whether the ground investigation report is adequate.
This is the first step.
In the design process, the settlement check comes before sizing the foundation area.
It comes after: the stresses and settlements are calculated from the chosen dimensions.
Structural design (concrete grade, reinforcement) is the last step of the design process.
Before it, stability and uplift are also checked.
The depth of foundation is the vertical distance between the foundation level and the original ground surface.
It is the distance between the final ground surface and the foundation level.
In cohesive soil above 500 m above sea level, the frost depth is 1.0 m.
For a foundation on solid rock, the frost depth is 0.8 m.
In granular soil the frost depth is always 0.8 m; it cannot be varied.
Below 500 m above sea level it can be reduced to 0.5 m if the winter groundwater comes no closer than 2.0 m to the foundation level.
Ice lenses need frost-susceptible soil, a supply of water and a descending frost front.
If any of them is missing, no significant frost heave develops.
The foundation level should preferably be designed below the groundwater level, because the soil is denser there.
Preferably above the groundwater – dewatering is expensive.
On clay that changes volume, the foundation level must be designed below the desiccation depth (about 2 m).
Seasonal shrinkage and swelling act above this depth.
In stepped deepening, the line joining the corners may be at most 45°.
On sloping ground an inclined foundation level may be designed if the slope is small.
Never design an inclined foundation level; it must always be stepped.
On sloping ground, a single step should be no higher than 50 cm.
True: a higher step is not allowed on sloping ground.
The foundation level of the new building may be above that of the neighbour’s old building if the new building is lighter.
It must not be above the old one; it has to be deepened if necessary.
Bearing failure beneath the foundation is a GEO ultimate limit state.
The resistance is governed by the strength of the ground.
Unacceptable vibration is an ultimate limit state.
It is a serviceability limit state.
For shallow foundations, the GEO and STR limit states are the ones most often checked.
Bearing failure and the structural adequacy of the footing.
The risk of uplift (UPL) arises mainly for heavy structures above the groundwater.
For light structures reaching well below the groundwater.
The indirect method estimates the bearing resistance, for example, from penetration test results with an empirical formula.
Its advantage is less calculation.
In general shear failure the slip surface runs out to the surface and the ground heaves.
Typically on one side of the footing.
In punching shear failure there is a distinct peak on the load–settlement curve.
There is no peak there; the curve continues ever more steeply.
Shallow foundation
A foundation that transfers the load directly to the near-surface bearing stratum (within 1–2 m).
Deep foundation
A system founded on a deeper bearing stratum through a load-transferring element (pile, diaphragm wall, well or caisson foundation).
Deepened shallow foundation
A foundation built 3–5 m deep with shallow-foundation technology. It is designed as a shallow foundation, without shaft resistance.
Mixed (hybrid) foundation
A combination of shallow and deep foundations, e.g. a piled raft.
A footing, usually widened, providing continuous support for walls.
Rubble concrete
Concrete mixed with rubble stone (“cyclopean concrete”). The stone is in about half of the depth.
Pad foundation (block foundation)
A footing under columns and posts, usually square (B/L = 1–3.5).
A pocket for fixing a precast column. Today a pocket neck placed on a cast-in-place block footing.
A heavily reinforced ground beam connecting a row of columns in one direction.
Intersecting ground beams. It reduces differential settlement in both directions.
A continuous reinforced concrete slab running under the whole building. It supports both walls and columns.
Raft with hidden ribs
Only additional reinforcement is placed where the ribs would be; the thickness is constant.
Inverted floor
The reinforced concrete base slab of a building with a basement when the groundwater is high.
Ground-bearing raft
A reinforced concrete slab placed on compacted granular bedding; its underside may stay above the frost depth.
A monolithic box girder of the base slab, the basement walls and the floor acting together.
A slab with a curved surface in which only normal forces develop. It is no longer used.
Foundation level
The lower bearing surface of a shallow foundation, where it transfers the load to the ground.
Depth of foundation
The vertical distance between the foundation level and the final ground surface.
Frost depth
The greatest thickness of the soil layer that cools below 0 °C in winter (0.5–1.0 m in Hungary).
Ice lens
A layer of ice growing from water that seeps by capillary action to the frost front. The main cause of frost heave.
Desiccation depth
The depth (about 2 m) down to which clay that changes volume dries out and swells seasonally.
Natural slope
The inclination at which the soil still stands by itself. The check line for a partial basement.
Underpinning
Underpinning the neighbouring old footing in sections with concrete when the new foundation level is deeper.
High-pressure grouting that forms columns of soil-concrete. Also used to strengthen old foundations.
Ultimate limit state (ULS)
Failure or severe damage; GEO, STR, EQU, UPL, HYD.
Serviceability limit state (SLS)
Excessive settlement, differential settlement, vibration or heave.
Failure or excessive deformation of the ground.
Internal failure or excessive deformation of structural elements.
Loss of static equilibrium as a rigid body.
Loss of equilibrium due to uplift.
Direct method
A separate calculation model for each limit state (failure mechanism, settlement calculation).
Indirect method
Based on experience and measurements (e.g. penetration tests), with empirical formulae.
Prescriptive method
With a presumed bearing resistance, mainly for foundations on rock.
Consequence class (CC)
Classification according to the consequences of failure (CC1–CC4).
Geotechnical Category
The geotechnical classification of the structure (GC1–GC3). In the new EC7 it follows from the CC and the geotechnical complexity together.
Material factor and resistance factor approaches to verification in the new EC7.
A slip surface running out to the surface, heave, a peak on the load–settlement curve.
A partly developed failure surface, larger settlement, no peak.
Failure without a failure surface, with large settlement, in loose or soft soil.
Density index (ID)
ID = (emax − e)/(emax − emin). The state of density of a granular soil.
Active wedge, radial shear zone and passive wedge – the basis of the bearing resistance formula.
